speechtext: My hou. friends from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and Victoria (Mr. Sam. I-received a memorandum of his inquiries from the hon. member for North Toronto, and I would ask the hon. member for Victoria to be kind enough to put his inquiries in brief written shape, that I may be able to better guide the officers of the department in collecting the information. In regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for North Toronto that the procedure for the issue of a title in connection with the scrip issues under discussion should be delayed, I think it would be fair to draw a distinction between the question of the policy and administration of the department, and the question of the propriety of action on the part of those who are interested in securing the scrip. The department, I take it. is bound to carry on its affairs, and if the orders for scrip are in, and they seem to be legitimate and according to the rules of the department, it is scarcely in order to ask that delay should be made simply because the policy of the administration of the department is called in question. If there is a definite allegation of fraud in connection with this scrip, then certainly I would say it was necessary that the issue should be delayed ; but I would like to have the distinction sharply drawn between a definite allegation of fraud on the part of some person or persons more or less known, and a calling in question of the policy and administration of the department.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) is a little in error yet. No assignments have been accepted on tbe letter authorizing agents to accept. Nor are they authorized, if I followed tbe papers correctly when they were in my possession, to accept entry in the name of any other than the half-breed to whom the scrip was issued. All the difference is that he is not required to be there in bodily presence, but there is no change of ownership as between tbe scrip and tbe land. It has always been the rule, as stated in the papers, and, as I believe is the fact, that the scrip is issued to the half-breed who is entitled to it. It is issued in his name, and entry is made in his

name, and, until the patent is issued for the land no transfer can be made and no assignment is recognized under any of the Orders in Council, departmental letters or system of administration.

I submit to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and to hon. gentlemen on the other side, that this discussion is altogether premature. It is impossible to discuss the matter intelligently in all its bearings until all the papers have been brought down. In proof of this I would call the attention of the hon. member for North Toronto to the statement he made a moment ago with regard to the provision in the Order in Council of August, 1904, which he says-and says truly-allowed assignments to be made. But I would say to my hon. friend that, if my memory serves me well, this provision of the Order in Council of August, 1904, was rescinded in' the Order in Council of December 17, 1904.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think not- that is the impression I have of it. If I am wrong it only goes to justify what I have already said, that it is not' .possible to discuss this question until all the papers have been brought down. There was one point spoken of by my hon. friend, and I am not prepared to say what is the condition of affairs with regard to it, and that is the dispensing with the order which made it obligatory upon the half-breed to go and locate his own scrip. As to that, I do not know the reason which has led the department to change the policy, and cannot, at the moment, discuss the matter. But I have no doubt that there is some good and valid reason for it, and that this will appear when the papers are brought before the House. I would make one observation on the main point-and the only point made by my hon. friend from North Toronto, if I understood him correctly, the only one he sought to make to-day. This was to persuade the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to stay his hand aud stop at once the issue of these patents. Well, I think the reason given by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior for the position he takes is a very good one. He stated that if the object of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is to traverse the policy of the department, he has not shown that the suggestion should be adopted ; on the other hand if there is evidence or even allegation of fraud, that would be a very good reason why the issuing of patents should be stopped. But my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) would not take the responsibility of saying absolutely that there is evidence of fraud. He says there is a presumption of fraud. That may be. I have no doubt that if my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), on looking at the papers, finds pre-209
sumptive evidence of fraud, he will act accordingly. I believe the hon. member for North Toronto is quite sure that if the minister finds any evidence or even presumption of fraud he will act accordingly. To my mind, from the evidence we have and from the information available, the only fact which gives evidence of fraud, or upon which even a presumption of fraud can be based, is that the scrip will not be very profitable to the half-breeds. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) stated a moment ago that probably not more than one-tenth of the scrip will avail to the halfbreeds and that nine-tenths will be squandered. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior will have this answer to the leader of the opposition-that ever since scrip was first issued to the half-breeds, that is since the year 1870 or thereabouts, there has not been a single issue of scrip to these people that has not been squandered by them. Whenever there was an issue of scrip there was always a following of sharks after these people to get their scrip from them for a mere song-the half-breed got nothing for it. But we had this satisfaction, that, even if the half-breeds did not profit by it, at least, when we had given them the scrip they had no grievance. Blit until the scrip was given them they had a grievance-and we know the consequence of that kind of thing. I remember very well that Archbishop Taehe, and Father La-combe, and Lord Strathcona when his assistance was sought on these matters, took the ground that the scrip should be nontransferable. Well, we acted upon this policy in 1899, when we made the last previous issue of scrip. We issued a commission, of which Mr. Laird was a member, as also were Father Lacombe and Mr. McKenna and one or two others. They were to negotiate a treaty in Athabaska with the Indians. They were to collect the Indians and half-breeds and give scrip to those who had not participated in the distribution of 1885. My hon. friend remembers the result, for he alluded to it yesterday. We gave special instructions to make this scrip-land scrip-non-transferable. And what took place? Why, the Indians would not participate in the treaty, and the halfbreeds would not take their scrip, unless the scrip were made transferable. And we have the report-a report sent under emergency by the commissioners-that the half-breeds would use their influence with the Indians to prevent the signing of the treaty, and the half-breeds themselves would not take the scrip, unless it was made transferable. And the members of the commission who were there, Father Lacombe himself among them, then and there, to satisfy the half-breeds, asked that the scrip should be made transferable. Most of that scrip was squandered, no doubt. At the same time, by doing what we did. by adopting this policy which results in little benefit to

The half-breeds, we satisfied them as a class. [DOT]My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said that he did not think that there were any more half-breeds who had claims. He said that after the report had been made by the commission in 1899-1900, the halfbreeds who had been in the United States could not participate in this scrip and that they had forgotten everything about it. Well, he was given an answer by my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron) who called the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the fact that there are certain half-breeds in his own riding who claim that they did not receive the satisfaction to which thev were entitled
I do not understand that they were half-breeds who had crossed to the United States and gone on reservations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know about that. I only am trying to show that when the hon. gentleman says the halfbreeds had forgotten about this matter, he is mistaken. I am sure of one thing- though without having looked into the mat-ter-that there is good reason to believe that the half-breeds in the United States were claiming their scrip. I know that there is a close connection between the halfbreeds on one side of the line and the halfbreeds on the other side, and we have found it good policy, and I think it is good policy when we pay the half-breeds, even though they will get but a mere pittance of what is given out of the public treasury, still we find it good policy to give this scrip so as to prevent them from having a grievance which they can proclaim and parade in the Territories. As I said a moment ago, the policy is all right, and I believe we will be able to vindicate it triumphantly when the discussion comes on. My hon. friend has made the point that the halfbreeds allow other parties to locate land scrip for them. When the time comes we will give an explanation of that also, as of everything else.

^ Mr. W. H. BENNETT (East Simcoe). This morning I communicated with the Department of Public Works my intention to ask this afternoon a question relative to tenders for the government dock in the town of Collingwood. Lately so many matters are brought up ini the House, which perhaps may be characterized as scandals, that one seems to get inundated with letters from different parts, particularly I speak of the province of Ontario, in reference to matters in which the general public apparently think there is not exactly fair dealing. Perhaps the minister who may be acting to-day for the Minister of Public Works in his absence, may be able to give a satisfactory explanation of the matter to which I wish to draw attention. In the Collingwood ' Bulletin ' of Thursday, May 25, I find the following :
Tendering too low for public works is evidently an unsatisfactory way of doing business, and judging by late developments Messrs. Conroy Brothers, whose tender here for the proposed wharf here was accepted by the Department of Public Works at Ottawa, have found this to be too true to their sorrow. Their tender is said to have been $25,000, but upon investigation they discovered that there would be no money in the contract at that figure, but what could be done ? The department had accepted their figure, but above this it had the firm's marked cheque for $4,000 which would be forfeited were they to get out. They considered and hesitated, but evidently got from under, a letter from L. G. McCarthy to the chairman of harbour and frontages stating that they had declined to sign the necessary documents. Mr. McCarthy also stated that it was expected that the contract would go to the Battle Estate of Thorold, the next lowest tenderers, and that he hoped to see the matter definitely settled within a few days. This firm's tender is in the neighbourhood of $30,000.
May I ask the member of the cabinet who js acting on behalf of the Minister of Public Works, as to who Conroy Bros, are, where they reside, and if the statement I have read is true, and the suggestion thrown out here that owing to their being the lowest tenderers, their $4,000 cheque was returned. I may have some further remarks to make after the minister has answered these questions.

Group N was a new group that was formed. Up to this time group M was the last group they had, but they specially got up a group to cover Fredericton, Marysville and Gibson and it says :
The following stations will take group ' N,' Fredericton rates : Fredericton, Gibson and Marysville, New Brunswick. First-class rate 66 cents.
Here we have the Grand Trunk Railway tariff showing that the increased rate applies to Fredericton, Gibson and Marysville. And jet in the face of that, the minister occupied the time of the House for a couple of hours on the 17th of May stating emphatically out of the mouths of his officers, that there was no change in tariff to any point but Fredericton while in this very tariff which I will send over to the minister he will find that the rate to Fredericton, Gibson and Marysville is 66 cents as compared with 58 cents prior to the acquisition of the Canada Eastern. I want to put myself right befbre the House and the country for I never make a statement that I do not feel satisfied is correct. I was absolutely correct and the Minister of Railways was absolutely wrong, and he made a statement that he and his officers ought to have known was not correct when he made it.

It. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals). I am afraid my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is somewhat extravagant m his- remarks this afternoon. He started out with saying that I occupied the time of the House recently for three hours in trying to prove that he was wrong, but he qualified that statement later on by bringing it down to two hours.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: * Hansard ' will not show that I said three hours ; I said from two to three hours.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Now that my hon. friend has got it down to two hours, perhaps he might throw a little off that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No ; I think the discussion, lasted that long.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Be that as it may, what are the facts ? During the course of a debate some weeks ago the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) made certain statements in connection with freight rates on the Intercolonial Railway, and after expressing some surprise at his statements I promised to give him the information later-not to prove that lie v as not correct but to give the explanation ot the officials of the railroad. I communicated "with the traffic manager and he wrote me in reply a letter which I asked the Mr. TAYLOR.
permission of the House to read. In that reply the traffic manager stated in effect, that all points between Fredericton and Chatham Junction were on the same basis as they had originally been ; that is, they were put in the Moncton zone of freight rates. On that authority I made the statement.
Mr. TAY'LOR. Not Moncton but St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Moncton and St. John are on a par ; and things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
Correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I thought I had remembered it correctly. The point I was making is :-and my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) proves it-that it was by the action of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: With the consent and approval-

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, not with the consent, hut as against the protest of the Inter-colonal Railway traffic official, they had arbitrarily fixed the rate to Fredericton ; and they were enabled to do so by reason of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway reached Fredericton. I assume that the traffic manager, in writing to me, did not take into consideration the fact that Gibson is connected directly with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and therefore the Canadian Pacific can control the Gibson rates in the same way they can control the Fredericton rates. And Marysville

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: May I ask the minister why he was so emphatic in reply to the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) and the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) saying that it did not apply to Marysville and Gibson ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I made that statement because of the statement in the letter of the traffic manager to the effect that the points between Fredericton and Chatham Junction were not affected.
Is it because the Canadian Pacific Railway directly touches Fredericton and Gibson that they are able to control Intercolonial rates at these points ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is because the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as I understand it, have entered into an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway as to freight originating west of Montreal. Marysville is not directly on the Canadian Pacific Railway, but is distant a mile or thereabouts-it is within cartage distance.
It is three miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not from where their station is ?
Yes, it is certainly three miles to Fredericton.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am not as familiar with it as my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket), but it is within cartage distance. In Fredericton there are factories to which freight would have to be carted almost the same distance as to Gibson or Marysville. But it is because of this position that the freight rates are made the same as for Fredericton- that the Canadian Pacific Railway controls the situation and they can by arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway change these rates. But from the points which the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot touch, that is points on the Intercolonial Railway which are not affected by compact with the Canadian Pacific Railway, the rates are precisely the same. Take Bolestown for instance or Cross Creek, or Stanley

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The tariff gives all these.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes. All these points which are not controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway and cannot in any sense be the subject of contract between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, have the same rates as before. Therefore, substantially what I stated is proved by the explanation of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And so is the statement I made. But what I want to ask is whether the Railway Commission approved of these two new tariffs issued by these companies, that of the Canadian Pacific Railway on November 16, taking effect next day and one of the Grand Trunk Railway on March 17 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am not aware whether they were approved by the Railway Commission or even considered by them. I know that the railways have the right to file with the Railway Commission joint tariffs ; and until that commission takes action, either amending or revising that tariff1, it would be effective. Whether they did file these tariffs, as provided by the law, or not, I am not personally informed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will he ascertain whether they have been filed and approved and how long the government is going to allow them to run until they are approved of ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The government has no right to affect that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The government can control the Railway Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The government does not control the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission is an independent body ; it stands independent of the government, the railways and the patrons of these railways. Any shipper on the line of any of these roads has the right to ask the commission to revise the tariffs. It is true that the Minister of Railways can ask the Railway Commission to take action and decide matters to which his attention is called. But the government has no control of the decisions of the commission, nor does it decide
the time when such matters should be taken up. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) has not in any way maintained his original position. He undertook to say that the freight rates from Trenton and Sydney . to Brockville and Gananoque were greater than they were from Gananoque or Brockville to Pittsburg.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: At 37 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I did not take um-barge at my hon. friend making such a statement. Of course I should have been surprised to find the hon. gentleman's information correct. I made inquiry and found that the distance between Trenton and Brockville was very much greater than the distance between Pittsburg and Brockville.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I did not complain of that; what I complained of rvas the 37 cents to Gananoque-25 cents and 12 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: But he undertook to east reproach in some way upon the Intercolonial by reason of that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Upon the combine. Because, I consider you are all in an arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
But the facts show that my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is not looking at it in the right spirit.
Mr. TAYLOR, I am one of the sufferers.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that this carload to which he refers wras billed from Trenton to Brockville. The car reached Brockville, and the Intercolonial had nothing to do with it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) cannot expect the rate to Gananoque to be the same as the rates to Brockville. An important point like Brockville of course, must have a different rate from a place like Gananoque.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: After the car had reached Brockville the consignee, I understand, desired to have it sent on to Brockville. It was subject to local rates over the Grand Trunk Railway from Brockville to Gananoque. No reproach can be cast on the Intercolonial for discrimination on the part of the Intercolonial in such a case.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I brought it up in order that the Railway Oommission_ might consider the grievance-a rate of 25 cents from Trenton to Brockville and 12 cents for the thirty miles to Gananoque.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) knows that there is a great distinction between the through rate and the local rate. He must have known indeed that if these statements were not true he was doing a great injustice to the management of the Intercolonial in bringing the name of that railway into question at all. The way he

placed the matter before the House would lead one to conclude that the Intercolonial was at fault, that the officers of the Intercolonial were discriminating unfairly in the application of freight rates. I so understood him, and I asked for an explanation, because it is my desire, so far as I am responsible for the administration of that railway, that the rates shall not be discriminatory, that they shall be fair and equitable to all sections of country so far as it is possible to make them so. I am glad my hon. friend has made this explanation, he has clearly proved that the Intercolonial is not at fault, that the Intercolonial is not responsible for-increased rates to and from Fredericton, or to and from points that are included within the Fredericton zone, and which are controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I thank him for bringing it to the attention of the House, and for emphasizing the fact that the Intercolonial is in no sense responsible for that increased rate on traffic originating west of Montreal.

During the discussion of this matter the other day I asked the Minister of Railways if the increase applied only to Fredericton, and he informed me then that it did, and that there was no increase to Marysville or to Gibson. Now the statement of the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) indicates that the minister was mistaken in the answer he gave to my question. I may say in connection with this matter, that the council of the Fredericton Board of Tr-ade had a meeting on Wednesday night, and I have here a copy of the Fredericton ' Gleaner ' of last night, containing _an account of that meeting. It was stated in the course of the discussion here that the merchants of Fredericton had agreed to this increase in the Fredericton rates. At the time I was at a loss to know why they should have done so, because the letter which the minister read from the general traffic manager of the Intercolonial stated that the Intercolonial authorities themselves considered that the discrimination against Fredericton was most unfair. In the report of the meeting to which I refer, I find this :
Mr. Hodge stated that Messrs. Randolph, Sterling, himself and other men had complained at the differential of three cents per hundred weight over the rate on all freight from Montreal and points west of Montreal to St John, Moncton and other places with which they had always enjoyed the same rate. They later met the Canadian Pacific Railway officials, and after a conference decided to accept the differential on all other classes of goods providing that they got the same rate on grain produce that St. John, Moncton and other places enjoyed.
Mr. Randolph explained that the Canadian Pacific Railway had claimed that -they had changed their rates from Fredericton north and that that justified them in raising the rate on freight coming in. The merchants claimed that this was not fair and the changes did not bring it down as far as a mileage basis. When the Mr. EMMERSON.
Canadian Pacific Railway officials offered to put the rates on grain back the merchants felt that it was better to take that offer than nothing at all. A month or so later Mr. Randolph's firm wrote complaining of the arrangement to the general freight agent of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Mr. Randolph pointed out that for a long haul to Sydney the rate was the same as to Fredericton.
So it seems that the wholesale grocers of Fredericton did assent to the rate being maintained, to the increase being maintained, on other classes of goods than on grain products, because they could do no better. But the board of trade, at a meeting, ou Wednesday, passed a strong resolution protesting against this discrimination. I may say that the people of Fredericton feel that the discrimination is most unfair and unjust. It is not only the merchants of the city of Fredericton who are interested in this matter, but it is the people who purchase the goods ; the farmers, the mechanics and the labourers of the city of Fredericton and the county of York are paying this increase, and the whole community is very much opposed to this discrimination, and very much disappointed that it has resulted from the acquisition by the government of the Canada Eastern Railway. The great argument, I may say, that was made iu the county of York with reference to the acquisition of the Canada Eastern Railway by the government was that if the government did not acquire it the Canadian Pacific Railway would, and that we would be entirely in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to freight rates. It is rather disappointing then to say the least, to hear the admission made upon the floor of this House by the Minister of Railways that the Canadian Pacific Railway now controls the freight rates of the Intercolonial to Fredericton-that is the admission which I understand the minister to make that at Fredericton and all points that are touched directly by the Canadian Pacific Railway, that road determines the rate. That is a matter of great disappointment to the people of Fredericton. Now the correspondence which the minister referred to the other day shows that, as I said before, the Intercolonial authorities themselves recognize the injustice of the discrimination, and I do hope that the Minister of Railways will exert his influence to have that discrimination removed as speedily as possibly.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Debates-amount required to cover expenditure for session of 1904 paid during present financial year, $31,503.74.
What was the main vote ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is largely owing to the fact that the session of 1904 was so long. The session was estimated at 130 days, but it exceeded that by 41 days. These 41 days had to be taken into con-

sideration this year. The items are as follows : Amanuenses for ' Debates ' reporters during the extra period, $1,291.50; printing and binding, printing paper, $29,066.01. This represents the accounts of the Printing Bureau for work done after the first of July, 1904. to the end of the session. Seven hundred dollars is for the preparation of the analytical index. The Debates Committee ordered this index to be prepared last year.
That is the index of the ' Hansard ? '

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

Is it being carried out this year as I think it was last year, namely, that the whole index is not in each volume of the ' Hansard.' I want to call the attention of the speaker and the committee to this, because it seems to me to be a very inconvenient way. I send for the ' Hansard,' quickly or not in order to look for a certain thing. I do not know how many volumes of the ' Hansard ' I may be obliged to get before I get the particular volume that I want. It used to be always so that no matter what volume of the 'Hansard ' you got you had the complete index of all the volumes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that is still so.

No, as I understand it now, you do not have a complete index in every volume of the ' Hansard.' You have an index for each volume, and consequently you may have to send for and look up all the volumes before you get the one you want. That is very inconvenient and I do not think the little amount of expense that would cover the paper, because that would be about what it would be, is a sufficient reason why we should not have a complete index in every volume.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is in error about that, although I speak with some hesitation about it, but my recollection, being then a member of the Debates Committee, was that the intention was that each volume, consisting of approximately 2,000 columns and being of a uniform size, should have an index of the contents of that volume, the complete index of all the volumes to be in the last volume.
That is what I mean ; you only get the complete index in the last volume.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Oh, yes, I see. You want the index in all ?

I want it in all. It is now very inconvenient.
Mr. SPEAKER, The idea of the committee at that time, as I well recollect, was that it would be a very convenient thing to have the bound volumes of the * Hansard ' put into the hands of the members at the earliest possible date. If that is done it is manifestly impossible to have a complete index in each because the complete index cannot be ready until all the volumes are out. The idea of the committee was that, instead of having these loose volumes prepared by the pages, a volume of
2,000	columns should be printed and bound and placed in the hands of members, rather than, as has been the custom, that they receive these volumes two or three months after the session was over. That was what the committee had in view and the change was made for that reason. If it is not considered wise to take that course it would be a proper thing to refer the matter back to the Debates Committee to consider it further. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor), who is a member of the committee, will probably remember the reasons which actuated the committee in making the change.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We have our hands full of trouble on the Debates Committee every session. Last session a change was made. The government appeared to have had a gentleman that they had to find a job for in the person of Mr. McGillicuddy, and it was suggested to change the system of indexing the ' Hansard.' It was proposed that we should get up an analytical index, he was engaged to do it and the whole system was changed. But, the members found It was so inconvenient that at the first meeting of the Debates Committee this year we changed the system and went back to the old system, and in every volume of ' Hansard ' for this year and future sessions, until the government have another gentleman that they want to find a job for, there will he found a complete index. The Debates Committee recommended and the House has approved of it, that we should revert to the old system of having a complete index in every volume of 'Hansard.' That will go into operation this session.
Committees-additional amount required, $2,-
000.
What is the explanation of that ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is in connection with reporting and the payment of witness fees for the Telephone Committee and the Agriculture and Colonization Committee.
Stationery-additional amount required, $10,000.
What was the main vote for stationery?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have not that at hand.
The reason that this additional vote is asked is owing to the length of the last two sessions. The stock was very much reduced, and then the Toronto fire prevented the stationer from securing from local people the necessary supply with the result that quite a lot had to be imported
<5595

from Massachusetts and heavy express charges had to be paid upon it. But, the principal reason why this additional vote was required, was because of the length of the last two sessions, one of five months and the other of seven. The main estimate I find now was $15,300.

I would call the attention of the committee to the quality of some of the note paper which is supplied to members of the House. I have made application for paper over and over again and I have been supplied with paper of a very poor quality. I have been supplied with paper which was not worth more than two or three cents or at the most five cents a quire. On one occasion when I sent for note paper I was told that all the note paper was in our boxes. I think there is a great deal of favouritism and partiality shown in the stationery office.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will call the attention of the stationer to the hon. gentleman's remarks.
Sessional clerks, $11,700.
What was the original vote for that ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: What Is the cause of that ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The same remark I made a little while ago in connection with another item, that is the extra length of the session of 41 days to be provided for this year, applies to this.
How many sessional clerks have we ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are 30.

Now will the Speaker tell us what is the duty of those clerks, whom do they serve and at whose wishes do they do their work ? I would like to know and I do not know what the position is, whether the members are to get any use of them or have they special duties or how is it ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: These clerks are strictly under the direction of the clerk of the House and their first duty is to serve requests from the House, to prepare papers, copy papers, or do any departmental work of that character.
That is from the clerk of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
From the clerk of the House, which is called for by reason of the action of the House. Then if they have any extra time, as they frequently have, it litis been the custom, us far as I can gather, for them to serve members. Any statements or copies in connection with departmental documents that are asked of it is their duty if they have the leisure The SPEAKER.
time to prepare at the request of the members. They are liable of course to be called upon to attend on the select committees and to prepare statements, documents, or serve them in any way. These are in a general way the duties of the sessional clerks.
These sessional clerks are all clerks. They do not do the work of messengers or anything like that ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No.
What is the legal number provided for ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am informed by the clerk that there are 30 sessional clerks.
And you have now ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have a full list of 30.
I think the statement was made that the sessional clerks were 52.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The messengers alone are 52.
I am not speaking of the messengers. We are on the vote for sessional clerks and I asked how many sessional clerks there were and the answer I got was 52.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is wrong, there are 30.	28 permanent sessional clerks and 2
extra sessional clerks.
How many sessional clerks are being paid out of this vote ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: These 30.
And are there not more than 30 ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. There are no more sessional clerks than these.
This vote that is now being taken is simply to pay for the 30 sessional clerks and for no other service ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: For no other service for the extra 41 days.

For the extra 41 days and for the 41 days you want a vote of $11,700 for clerk hire ? And for an ordinary session you take a vote of $13,810. That does not seem to quite fit in. Forty-one days as compared with the ordinary session ought not to give an increase of $11,700. That would give for 30 clerks a large amount of money.

As I make it the total vote of the main estimates with the vote now asked of $11,700 will make a total of about $24,000. The session lasted about 180 days and the sessional clerks are paid $4 a day. That would make $120 a day and if you multiply 120 by 180 you have a total of the two estimates about $21,000.

What I was getting at was that if it requires $11,700 for 41 days,

if the original vote contemplating the usual session, called for $13,810 it ought not to take $11,700 to cover the extra 41 days.

The hon. gentleman will see at once that $13,000 would not cover a session to which would be added 41 days. In other words the original estimate of $13,000 was not sufficient for the session lasting as the one we had last year lasted.
Who made the estimate for last year ?
I forgot ; the Speaker or probably the clerk.
Why does the Speaker bring before the House an estimate which he knows is not sufficient for the ordinary session ?

Because the estimate has always been based for years and years on a session of a certain number of months. The session last year not only was 41 days .onger than usual, but more than twice 41 days, so that the original estimate was found to be far out, owing to the extra time.

I presume the intention of the government was to have a very short session when they brought that in. They did not intend to inflict that iniquity on the Northwest. Now they realize that the snow is likely to fly before they get away.
This is last year.
It will take possibly until next Christmas to explain to the people of the country-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is very clear.	i
What is very clear that a great iniquity is being perpetrated on the Northwest.
Better make the estimate for a year now to be sure for the future. Where are these sessional clerks to be found; have they a room in the building here ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

Are they for the use of members for anything connected with the House ? If we have any translation to make or anything of the sort can we get that work done by them instead of paying out of our own pockets to have it done ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I explained a few moments ago in the absence of my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) that the first duty of these clerks is to serve the House and to serve any committee of the House in the preparation of information or documents and if they have time, as they frequently have, beyond that it is their duty to attend upon requests of members of the House, prepare
documents or statements for them or anything of the kind they can do.
Those for the committees as far as I can remember are old permanent clerks who are clerks of the Committees. They are to be found in the committee rooms where they act as secretaries.
Are they sessional clerks?

No, I would call them permanent employees, the clerk of the Agricultural, Railway, Standing Order or other committee would lie a permanent employee.
I am talking more especially of the sessional clerks. I may say I do not know where they are and I very seldom see them. I am asking this because very often we have some translation to do. To-day I have some translation to do and I have either to pay for it or do it myself if I have time.
I ask that as a matter of information.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think they could be called on to do that. It depends altogether on how much of their time Is taken up in the direct service of the House for which they are procured.
What I would like to know is, what is this direct service which requires the employment of thirty-two sessional clerks ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If papers are called for by the House, they make copies of these.
Not returns from the departments ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, copies of these. The department makes one copy, and further copies are made by the sessional writers ; perhaps half a dozen copies are called for. A great deal of their time is taken up in that way. I do not think that they could be called on to do any work that members might wish them to do ; but if they have leisure, they might accede to the request of members who want them to prepare matters of that kind. They occupy a room near the entrance to the gallery, where they are provided with desks and typewriters.

We have had these thirty-two men employed for a long time, and the House has never yet had any return showing the services they have rendered. Could we not he informed just how many copies of reports they have turned off in the course of a session ? For instance, we ask for a return ; the minister lays it on the table of the House, and the clerk may ask me if I would like a copy of it. If I said I would, that is the work of a sessional clerk. When a return is brought down to the House, it is either printed or not printed. If it is not printed, I undertake to say that very few copies are required by the members during a session. 1 do not know that in the years that I have sat in the House I have ever asked for a copy of any of these papers to be made for me by the sessional clerks, and

I think that is true of most of the members. The conclusion I have come to-it may be wrong-is that for thirty-two clerks the amount of work taken out of them in preparing duplicates for the use of members is comparatively very little, and I would like to have a return of the work that is really turned out by them. We should not have thirty clerks and not keep any tab over them so as to know what they are doing. When you take away that work, what other work is there for these men to do ? In the twenty years that I have been in the House I have never had any sessional clerk do any work for me. If other members are in the same position, what are these clerks doing ? But if some members have work done by them, and know how it is done, could we not have a director of sessional clerks to whom any member could apply when he wanted the services of a clerk ? For instance, if I want a piece of work done, I do not want to go to the rooms and hunt up a clerk for that purpose. If there were a director of the clerks, I could go to him. As it is, if we pay clerks we ought not to have to waste our own brain and nerve energy in preparing statements, so Jong as they have leisure to do it. Is there any method, and if so, what is the method that is adopted in that respect ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I said a little while ago, they are, in the first instance, under the Clerk of the House, to whom application can be made by members at any time for copies of documents ; and I am told by the clerk that application is frequently made to him and also direct to members of the staff of sessional clerks. There is a chief of that staff, Mr. Stewart, and applications can be made to him at any time in the same way. I should have said also that eight members of this staff are assigned to the post office in the House, and are there practically all the time sorting. I think there is a great deal in what the hon. member has said, that the House ought perhaps be better apprised as to what the duties of the sessional clerks are, and what reports and documents they have prepared, and I will ask the clerk to procure a statement to that effect and lay it before the House.
Is care taken to see that the sessional clerks are really men who are capable and can be trusted to prepare, for instance, a statement which I might want for use in the debate on the budget ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: So far as I can leam, they are all pretty reliable men. It may be that in the future more attention should be paid to their being stenographers or typewriters ; but, so far as I can learn, they ajegood, reliable, trustworthy men, capable of doing any reasonable work which a member might ask to have done by them. Of course, they are answerable for their conduct to their chief, and particularly to the Clerk of the House.
How can we know when they are at leisure ? There is no way of finding that out unless we ask every day.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the only way would be to apply to the chief.

I believe that they are available 'mostly to members on the government side. We do not have much benefit from them. With such a number of clerks, we should have our share of them whenever it Is necessary in the public service. I am told that in the Ontario legislature there are thirty clerks who are, I imagine, like these, paid by the House, and who are at the service of the members. If I am well informed, each of these clerks is at the disposal of three members. They are very good clerks, and the members utilize them. I would also call Mr. Speaker's attention to the fact that we are at a great disadvantage so far as accommodation is concerned. As to the messengers, I must say that they are really very attentive, but we have a good many round the House who seem to be assigned to some kind of special work. I have remarked during this session that the doors of the House are very badly kept. I have seen strangers ou the floor of the House, and it seems to me that should not occur when we have so many doorkeepers. I have seen men coming through those doors behind the Speaker's chair, and I have even seen a man sketching the House through the open doors. Indeed I have seen men at the back of the chamber, and on one occasion a man was smoking there. It seems to me that we have enough messengers to take care that the precincts of the chamber are kept sacred, and I would ask the Speaker to look into the matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The attention of the sergeant-at-arms has been called to the matter and I do not think my bon. friend will have cause to complain in future. It is proper that the chamber should be kept for the members, and that the corners should not be a loafing place for officials of the House or auy one else. There Is nu doubt that the accommodation for the sessional clerks is most miserable at present. These twrenty-two men are crowded into a room where they cannot live in comfort and health. 1 believe that question is receiving the consideration of the Department of Public Works together with the general question of better accommodation for the members of the House. As the business of the House has increased and the staff has been enlarged, there is a manifest lack of accommodation for the members, who have not at their disposal the facilities they should have for their comfort and convenience in the discharge of their duties. That whole question is at present engaging the attention of the Internal Economy Committee, and particularly the Minister of Public Works. I am in hopes that at some early day he will be able to make a statement to

the House which will be satisfactory to bon. gentlemen.

The sessional clerks have never refused to typewrite and give a copy of the returns laid on the table of the House, but as I understand it the hon. member for North Toronto was asking the Speaker whether the sessional clerks are competent to secure data for the budget speech for instance, or for a reply to the budget speech. Ho I understand Mr. Speaker to say they would be competent, and prepared to do that class of work ? Suppose a member wanted to make a search in the Library for some particular information, do we understand that it would be part of the duties of a sessional clerk to procure that information ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would not think that all of them would be competent to do that work, although I am perfectly satisfied that some of them are quite competent. It has come to my notice in previous years that they have done work of that class, but I cannot say at this moment how many of them would be capable of doing it.

Is it part of their duties to do that; and if it is a circular should be issued to every member of this House informing him of that fact, so that each member of the House should know exactly where he stands in regard to it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Their first duty is to the House, and one could only know definitely whether they could do that work by applying to the chief. If any members of the staff were at leisure at the particular time a member applied, I think their duty would be to serve that member and I think they would be willing to do so. If, however, it is to be a generally recognized rule that members may apply to these officials to do such work, the present staff would not be at all adequate and it would have to be largely increased.

I do not think these men should be allowed to do that sort of work for an instant. Last session, I do not know what it is this session, we had the respected Admiral from Goderich who was utilized by some members of this House to pick up data for them. It is all right for the First Minister to have Mr. Farrer to prepare his speeches and get data and that sort of thing, but I do not think this House should pay members of the Library staff or members of the sessional staff to procure information which may be used in speeches.
The gentleman you refer to was not a sessional clerk.
He was employed to do work he did not do ; he was employed by the Debates Committee and he did not do anything last year.

I have in my hands a note sent into the chamber last session drawing * Dear Sir William's ' attention to 210
a certain column in the ' Globe ' where he would find an item with which he could ' slug Sam.'
Who wrote that ?
Mr. McGillic-uddy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How did you get the note ?
The note was brought to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did he send it to you by mistake ?
You may be sure that he did not intend it to be sent to me, at all events the note is in my possession and 1 want the Minister of Finance to understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume you sent it to the proper person ?*
That would cut no ice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did he send it to you by another man's note.

I want these gentlemen to understand that they are not here to do work for members on the government side of the House, and I object to these sessional clerks being employed for any such purpose as hunting up data for the speeches of gentlemen opposite. If one member has a right to have that done, every member of the House has a similar right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The statement I made was that every member in the House should have the same right in the matter.
In justice to the gentleman referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) I should say that he was not on the staff of the sessional clerks, and he is not now.
What was he doing in the name of goodness ?

Last session the Debates Committtee recommended that he should be employed for the purpose of preparing an index of all sessional papers from the year 1894 to the present time. The last index of that kind was brought up to 1894 and on the recommendation of the Debates Committee this gentleman was employed to continue it. The index is prepared and is being printed now.
What is he doing now ?
I do not know. I am told he is employed by the Debates Committee.

That is not the information I have. I understand that this gentleman, together with a French gentleman, was employed last year to make an analytical index of ' Hansard,' which was a new idea. I may say that we have altered that a



little and gone back to the old system of having the index attached to each volume of * Hansard,' as the members desired and as X think is the better way. The French gentleman has done his work thoroughly, but the English gentleman of whom I spoke had mot done anything. The Debates Committee received a letter from that gentleman explaining that the reason why he had not done anything was that he had been sick, and we accepted that explanation. I have been told that during the time that he was supposed to be sick he was doing something else. X imagine that is what my hon. friend refers to.
Mr. BEX,COURT. The work he was required to do was undertaken because of a report in favour of it by the Debates Committee last session. The gentleman was here a part of the session and he was not receiving any salary or indemnity from the House or the government. Towards the close of the session the report of the committee was made to the House, and adopted in favour of having this index prepared. I was mistaken when I said a moment ago that it covered ten years. It covered fourteen years-from 1890 to 1904. The work has been completed and is being printed.
What is it ?
An idex of the sessional papers from 1890 to 1904-really an index of the journals of the House including the sessional papers and the Votes and Proceedings.
Was there no index of that ?
Up to 1890, yes ; but the last fourteen years had not been indexed.

Returning to the question of the sessional clerks, I would like to ask the Speaker if all these 32 men are employed in the sessional clerks' room ? I have gone in there frequently, but had no idea there were such a large number on the staff. Are any of them employed by the members in the different rooms ? Or, of course, they may work in relays, some in the early part of the day and some later, which would account for one not seeing so many in the room at once.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: A couple of these men are employed by the whips, one on either side. One of them is employed partly in attendance upon the deputy speaker's room and there are eight in the post office. Allowing for such cases, the number working in the sessional clerks' room would be about from eighteen to tweny-two.

I must say that I have always had a good deal of delicacy in ' asking any help of the sessional clerks, not knowing exactly what I had a right to expect. But it is only due to Mr. Stewart the chief of that staff, to say that I have always I Mr. BERGERON.
received the utmost courtesy and have never been refused anything I asked. At the same time I have avoided asking for the copying of documents in a good many cases not knowing what was my strict right. But, if we as members of the House are entitled to more privileges than I have hitherto claimed, I would be glad to be informed, for I would avail myself of them, being one of those who believe in taking all they can get. I have often wondered if the sessional clerks were available to assist in the private correspondence of members. We are called upon to WTite a great many letters, yet not in such fashion that we have continuous employment for a typewriter. To have the assistance of a clerk for one or two days in the week would be a great help.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If, on application to Mr. Stewart, the chief of the staff, it were found that members of that staff were available, I do not know why they should not be used for that class of work.

So far as the whips secretaries are concerned, they are overworked now!. Owing to their position they are called upon to work long hours, and a lot of work is imposed upon them. I think a great deal of this is due to the fact that members do not think they have a right to ask the ordinary sessional clerks to typewrite documents, and so the whips' secretaries are called uj>on to do the work. If it were better understood that sessional clerks generally could be called upon for that class of work, it would relieve these other officers of much of the work they are now called upon to do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: While I indicated that it is probably the right of members to avail themselves of the services of these officers, it must be apparent that with perhaps twenty clerks available, if 215 members exercise that right to any great extent, it would be impossible for these men to do much else than serve the members of the House. Of course, such work could only be expected of them when they have time to do it, and that can be ascertained by application to the chief of the staff. But where these clerks have the time, I do not see why their services should not be availed of in that way. The chief of the staff will see to it, I suppose, that they are not required to work too many hours in the discharge of their duties.

It seems to me that Mr. Speaker went a long way when he authorized the use of sessional clerks to assist in the private correspondence of members. I do not know where we should end if we began that. It seems to me that either we have too many clerks, or we have not enough, or we have not the right kind. The work of a working member of this House is very arduous. He has a large private correspondence that he is bound to take care

of. Then he has a large correspondence of a public nature that he has to take care of. Then, there is the work of the House. My own experience is that, as compared witli what it was fifteen or twenty years ago, the work of this House is very much increased. The multiplicity of things that claim our attention, the rapid succession in which new questions are forced upon us, make it arduous drudgery for even the best man to keep even with the work of the House. One almost feels like giving it up in despair and deciding to run the chance of making what show he can in the House with as small a modicum of work as possible. In some legislative assemblies they give every member a clerk or amanuensis. That seems extravagant at first blush, and it is certainly expensive. But to give each member a clerk or secretary may not in some respects be any more than the public man who gives his work to the House and country is entitled to. But we have not yet come to that, and it must be a good while before we will come to it.
But I think it is possible that if we had a staff of sessional clerks, the right men, competent, varied in their ability to work, stenographers, quick at summaries, calculating definitely and well, and doing their work so that it can be thoroughly relied on-I think there is a class of work that a moderately large number of clerks of the right kind could do for members, under the direction even of the clerk of the House, or of a director of the staff, divided so that it will be perfectly fair and even for both sides of the House, and all members of the House, a class of work that they might do with advantage to public business. Now something like this for instance : There was laid on my desk to-day six different returns with reference to certain subjects. Now, when I saw them my heart sank; I said to myself : How ever am I going to get through with that, analyse it and bring it here in the course of ten days or so, ready for the discussion which we have invited upon it ? For instance, it is relating to a matter which we were discussing to-day and yesterday. Now it would not be a partisan thing, I think, and it would be a public benefit, and would do a great deal to help the working members of the House, if, when a return like that comes down, they knowing what kind of information they want to get from it, a tabulation, were just to write a little memorandum of the tabulation they wanted in that return, and hand it over to a competent sessional clerk and have him make that tabulation. It would not be a partisan piece of work, you are not directing him as to what he shall say against the government or for the government, you are after a certain tabulation out of all these returns. I do not know whether I will ever get that done myself, if I have to do it. But there is a species of work which I
2104	/
should think a competent staff of sessional clerks could do, and do fairly well, and could alleviate the members of this House, for the public good and the public service. But if you come to say that we will have clerks here who will take up the private correspondence of members, I am afraid that we will go so far in that direction that it will simply become an impossibility, and will end in a worse state of affairs than we have to-day. But I would like, Mr. Speaker, and the clerk of the House to think it over, and see whether we can have, say, 25 or 30, or more if necessary, thoroughly good, first-class men, typewriters, stenographers, summarists, men who know just how to take hold of papers and give you a summary that you require out of them, and have them under competent direction and distribution to do work of that kind for the working members of the House. That is a thing which I think we might improve upon, because otherwise it comes to this, that even the best workers of the House, appalled by the tremendous amount of labour they have put upon them in order to get through the work, will fall behind hand in their work, and the public interests will suffer in that respect.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It will be apparent that the class of men the hon. gentleman refers to would have to be a superior class of men, and probably we would require to pay them a little more than we pay the present staff. Any one can see at once with what great utility they would serve various members of the House. The clerk of the House and myself will take the matter up and see if we can make some suggestion, at all events, to the House to be dealt with at some future day.
Leather trunks, 240 at $25 each, $6,000.
How is that thing carried out ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: According to a report of the Joint Committee on printing.
Who makes the trunks ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The contract is on tender, I understand, given out by the Printing Committee.
Is value got for these trunks ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: They seem to be very good.

Tenders were invited, and two houses tendered. They brought in some samples which were examined by a special committee of the Printing Committee and were found satisfactory. The contracts were given to two houses, and the members were invited to go and choose for themselves which house they should get their trunks from.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

After Recess.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 144) to incorporate the Fessenden Wireless Telegraph Company of Canada.-Mr. Geof-frion.
On sections 11 and 12,

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
When we last had this Bill under discussion clauses 11 and 12 were allowed to stand because there was a proposal made by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to add a word. I did not take upon myself at that time to accept the suggestion, because I was only acting for the promoter of the Bill, but since then I have been authorized by the hon. member for Chambly and * Vercheres (Mr. Geoffrion), who is in charge of this Bill, to accept the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Finance. Section 11 reads like this :	The company may enter into any
agreements with any government, and if I remember well the proposal of the Minister of Finance was to add the word ' Canadian ' so that it would have nothing to do with any foreign government. I therefore beg to move :
That the word ' Canadian ' be inserted before the word ' government' in the second line of section 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Is that word going to qualify * corporation ' and ' person ? '

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: The difficulty the other day was that in not mentioning which government was intended it might mean a foreign government, although I understand it means either this government or a provincial government, and the hon. Minister of Finance proposed, so that there should be no doubt about it, to put in the word ' Canadian ' before the word ' government.' 1 move to insert the same word in section 12.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Would it not be better to say ' any government in Canada ? '

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: It is only a matter of phraseology ; that is the meaning of it. By putting in the word ' Canadian government ' it serves also the purpose of qualifying the word ' corporation ' or ' person.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: If it is intended to give the company power to enter into agreements with the governments of any of the provinces, I think the expression ' Canadian government ' is not very appropriate.

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: How would it do to say ' with any Canadian government ?'

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: No, I would think that you might say, ' any government in Canada, or any provincial government/ Provincial governments are Canadian governments in a certain sense but they are not Canadian governments in the ordinary-sense.

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Well, put it in good English.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Is it the intention to restrict the words ' corporation ' or 1 person ' in the same way ?

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Not persons, but corporations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Would you make it read ' any government or corpo-ation in Canada ? '

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: All right. I will therefore move that sections 11 and 12 be amended by inserting in the second line of each after the word ' corporation ' the words ' in Canada.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: How will it read then ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: The company may enter into agreements with any government or corporation in 'Canada or person. &c.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: I do not think that is a very good way of wording it. The words ' in Canada ' might be held to apply to the verb enter into ' and not to ' government.' Why not say that they may enter into agreements with the government of the Dominion, or with any province or with any corporation or person ?

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: The clause as it stands is the very same clause that was in the Marconi Act. The other evening when it was suggested that these words be added I did not take it upon myself to accept them, but since I have been authorized to do so. It is the same clause that they have in the Marconi Bill. The Minister of Finance will remember that the other day when discussing the Fessenden Wireless Telegraph Company we left two clauses aside in order to consider the insertion of the word * Canadian ' before ' government,' to be sure that the company would not be dealing with a foreign government and we are moving to add these words now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: The member who has charge of the Bill and who, in his absence, has handed it over to my hon. friend, mentioned this to me to-day. I think that from any point of view we need not object on behalf of the government. Whether the amendment carries out as fully the intention of my hon. friend as he desires I do not know, but I do not see any objection to the suggestion of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) to insert the word ' Canadian ' before ' government.'

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: I would have preferred to have seen the whole power subject to the approval of the Governor in Gouncil, and then the powers could be made as wide as you like.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: The Bill already contains a clause with respect to the erecting of stations, and in the practical working out of the scheme they have to come to the Governor in Council, but this particular clause relates to agreements, and I do not think this is especially subject to the Governor in Council.

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: If the agreement clause is made subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, I see no objection to making it as wide as you please.

subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
Clause 19, which has been added, makes the whole Bill subject to the Governor in Council. You might put it this way :
The government of Canada or of any province in Canada or with any corporation or any persons, &c.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker suggests to me that it might read :
The company may enter into agreements with any government, corporation or person in Canada or any province thereof.
' In Canada ' might cover it without any reference to the provinces. The expression ' in Canada ' would apply not only to ' government,' but to the persons and corporations as well.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: I would think the intention would be very well carried out by putting in the word ' Canada ' before ' government.' You do not want to restrict the corporations or persons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: I think the company are content to have it in the form my hon. friend suggests.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FESSENDEN WIRELESS TELEGRAPH COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
The section will then read :
The company may enter into agreements with any government in Canada or with any corporation or person for the purpose, &c.
The same amendment will be made in section 12.
Sections, as amended, agreed to.
Bill, as amended, reported and read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: [u"We will proceed in supply and I would like if possible to dispose of the supplementary estimates. The largest of the items are in the Public Works Department, and I hope with the assistance of the deputy minister to be able to give the House all the information necessary so that we may get a supply Bill through as early as possible.\nHa\u2122- R0,Y<:1E' ,Witb regard to the oth papers, if the hon. gentleman reads t Mr. BOYCE."]

In regard to these items under the heading ' sergeant-at-arms,' I desire to ask Mr. Speaker what the present position of the sergeant-at-arms is in regard to purchases for the House of Commons. It will be recollected that (last year a discussion occurred upon this subject, and as I understand, the position taken then was that up to a very recent period the sergeant-at-arms had been accustomed to make purchases, but that a year or two ago the Committee on Internal Economy had changed the position of the sergeant-at-arms in that respect, and while they left to him the care and custody of all property in the House, they made some change with regard to purchasing ; but there was some difference of opinion as to what the change really meant. It was said that the purchases in the future would have to be made under the direction of the committee and either the Speaker or the clerk. I am not sure which. But it was assumed by the then Speaker that that did not at all alter the duty or right or privilege of the sergeant-at-arms to make the purchases. That is, as I understood it, the sergeant-at-arms might still be considered to be the proper person to make the purchases, though lie might only make them under the immediate direction of the committee or Mr. Speaker or the clerk of the House. I would like to know exactly what the present position is, and what the intention for the future is in regard to such purchases ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think there is no very radical change in the matter. A resolution was passed to the effect, I believe, that before any purchases are made there must he a requisition from the sergeant-at-arms, who in the first place has to pass upon the propriety or impropriety of the

purchase ; and before he can purchase outright, this requisition must be passed upon by the Speaker or the Internal Economy Committee. As far as the act of purchasing is concerned, that is now as it has been always, done by the sergeant-at-arms, with this one qualification which was made a short time ago : There have been requisitions made to the department of the sergeant-at-arms for furniture by various members in connection with their rooms, and from time to time it appears that applications which either were or were not refused by the sergeant-at-arms branch were made to the Public Works Department in an indirect way-at all events not through the sergeant-at-arms-and were granted in some cases where they had not been granted by the sergeant-at-arms branch. This manifestly led to difficulty in keeping books and to the inconvenience of having applications made to one department after refusal by another. On consideration the Internal Economy Committee came to the conclusion that in the case of furniture, the requisition should first come from the sergeant-at-arms and be passed by the Speaker to the Department of Public Works. The purchase of furniture is now made entirely by the department of Public Works, but a written requisition must first be made by the sergeant-at-arms branch. All other supplies that have heretofore been purchased are still purchased by this branch and on the initiation of the sergeant-at-arms.
Do I understand that everything except furniture for rooms in the House of Commons is purchased by the sergeant-at-arms ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that is true.
Upon the requisition being approved the sergeant has absolute power to make the purchase and is the only-person authorized.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The requisition is made by him in the first instance and is passed upon by the Speaker, or, in case of a considerable amount, by the Internal Economy Committee. But in all cases except furniture the purchase is still made by the sergeant-at-arms.
What does Mr. Speaker mean by furniture for the House of Commons ? Does it include furniture for the members rooms and the furniture necessary for the work rooms of the offices and servants ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it includes all wooden furniture.
Does it take in furniture for the Speaker's rooms?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would take in what would come in under the term furniture.
Just wooden furniture ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, I think that is as far as the resolution goes.
Has Mr. Speaker a copy of the resolution ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I can get it in a few moments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is desirable that these regulations and orders made by the Internal Economy Committee should be laid before the House. I have been in the House nine years and I do not know anything about this committee, what it does or what its functions are, or what it is supposed to do. I never before heard of it doing anything, and I am much surprised to learn now that it has actually made an order about something.
